wine.name: Amarone della Valpolicella Classico
wine.classification: DOCG since 2010, from the historic Classico zone
wine.grapes: Corvina and Corvinone lead, with Rondinella and a small share of Cabernet, Nebbiolo, Croatina and Sangiovese.
wine.sites: The family's hillside vineyards around Negrar in the Classico zone, the oldest on Monte Ca' Paletta above the hamlet of Cerè, where the cellar and the family home stand.
wine.making: The grapes are dried for months in the estate's lofts, pressed no earlier than December as the appellation requires, and fermented slowly to dryness. The wine then rests about seven years in large casks of Slavonian oak before bottling. It is made only in years the family judges worthy; in other years the same dried grape wine becomes Rosso del Bepi.
wine.glass: Crushed and dried cherry, fig and dried flowers over exotic spice, cinnamon, cedar and woodland herbs, with citrus peel and a balsamic note for lift; full and warm, yet fresh, with fine tannin and a very long finish.
wine.ageing: Released many years after the vintage and ready to drink then, it keeps for many years more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; open or decant it an hour or two ahead, an old bottle gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The dry red of dried grapes, raised to DOCG with the decree of 2010.
From the historic hill communes of Valpolicella north west of Verona, Negrar among them.

label.term: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita
label.means: DOCG: Italy's guaranteed appellation, its rules set by decree.

records.table: Quintarelli's Amarone della Valpolicella Classico comes from the family's hills above Negrar: Corvina led grapes dried for months, fermented dry and kept about seven years in large Slavonian oak. Full and spiced yet fresh, it wants opening ahead and game or aged cheese.
records.story: The family began as sharecroppers: before the First World War the founder worked vines with his brothers at Figari, in the commune of Marano. In 1924 he moved to the Negrar valley and set up his own estate at Cerè, on the hill of Monte Ca' Paletta, where the family's oldest vines grow. His youngest son, Giuseppe Quintarelli (1927 to 2012), known as Bepi, took charge around 1950. He worked slowly: grapes dried in the lofts, years in large casks of Slavonian oak, about seven for the Amarone, and labels he drew and glued himself, as his obituaries recalled. In years the estate would not declare an Amarone, as in 2008 and 2010, the same dried grape wine went out as Rosso del Bepi, under his own nickname. Amarone della Valpolicella became a DOCG with the decree of 2010, and Bepi died in January 2012 at eighty four, after which the estate passed to his daughter's family. For a sommelier the wine marks the traditional pole of Amarone: unhurried, long in cask and late to release, the style against which modern, denser bottlings are set.

others.name: Rosso del Bepi
others.note: The Amarone grapes and method in years the family will not declare an Amarone, bottled as a Veneto IGT.

others.name: Alzero
others.note: Cabernet Franc dried and aged in the Amarone way, bottled as IGT and never called Amarone.

others.name: Recioto della Valpolicella Classico
others.note: The sweet wine of the same dried grapes, its fermentation stopped before dryness.

traps: Rosso del Bepi is declassified Amarone fruit and method, not a second wine from other vineyards.
Alzero is dried grape Cabernet Franc and may not be called Amarone, however it is made.
Amarone is dry; the sweet wine of the same dried grapes is Recioto della Valpolicella.

cards.front: Giuseppe Quintarelli: what is Rosso del Bepi?
cards.back: The estate's dried grape wine in years it will not declare an Amarone, such as 2008 and 2010, sold under Giuseppe Quintarelli's nickname.

cards.front: How long does Quintarelli's Amarone rest in large Slavonian oak casks before bottling?
cards.back: About seven years, far beyond the two years the appellation asks of an Amarone.

questions.q: Beside Corvina, Corvinone and Rondinella, which grapes play a small part in Quintarelli's Amarone?
questions.exp: The estate's Amarone carries a small share of Cabernet, Nebbiolo, Croatina and Sangiovese beside its Corvina led core; Garganega and Trebbiano di Soave are the white grapes of Soave.

questions.q: In some years Giuseppe Quintarelli would not declare an Amarone. Under which name did the same dried grape wine go out then?
questions.exp: Rosso del Bepi, named for Giuseppe's nickname, carries the Amarone grapes and method in years such as 2008 and 2010; Alzero is a dried grape Cabernet Franc.

Primal Wine: Giuseppe Quintarelli, the master of Valpolicella
Vinous: Quintarelli Amarone della Valpolicella Classico 2015
Consorzio Tutela Vini Valpolicella: Amarone della Valpolicella DOCG regulations

report: Eight searches of its own and one shared with Bertani on the Valpolicella consorzio's rules: the estate's own site returned nothing to a search restricted to its domain, so every fact rests on two secondary sources or the appellation body, with Nick's Wine Merchants and Superiore.de for Rosso del Bepi's years and IGT, Callmewine for the blend and the Grand Cru Wijnen and Nick's notes for the glass.

Founded is left empty, as in the library: the founder sharecropped at Figari before the First World War and set up his own estate at Cerè in 1924 (iDealwine, Primal Wine), so the story tells both rather than choose a founding year; the founder is described, his dates not found.
Bepi's dates rest on Decanter (dead in January 2012 at eighty four) and iDealwine (born 19 March 1927); his taking charge is given as 1950 and the early 1950s, so the story says around 1950.

The library's w-quintarelli-amarone says the grapes dry well into the spring; no source read gave the drying length, so the record says only for months, with the appellation's rule of no pressing before December.
The glass rests on two merchants' notes and the library's fig, balsamic and dried rose; no tasting note from the estate itself was found.

records.place: Grezzana, Valpantena, and Arbizzano di Negrar, Valpolicella, Veneto

wine.name: Amarone della Valpolicella Classico
wine.classification: DOCG since 2010, from the historic Classico zone
wine.grapes: Corvina Veronese, about four fifths, with Rondinella for the rest.
wine.sites: The Corvina vineyards of Tenuta Novare at Arbizzano di Negrar, in the Classico zone, which gave the first official vintage of the house's Amarone in 1958.
wine.making: The grapes dry through the autumn in the estate's lofts and are pressed in winter, no earlier than December as the appellation requires, then fermented slowly in concrete vats. The wine ages at least seven years in large casks of Slavonian oak, of fifty to one hundred hectolitres, in the historic cellar at Grezzana before release.
wine.glass: Plum, morello and dried cherry over tea leaf, liquorice and tobacco; dry and firm, with fresh acidity carrying the weight. With age it turns to dried fruit, medlar and truffle.
wine.ageing: Released only after its long years in cask and ready then, it keeps for decades: the house's own library of the wine runs back to the first vintage of 1958.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant an older bottle gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The dry red of dried grapes from the historic Classico zone, a DOCG since 2010.

label.term: Denominazione di Origine Controllata e Garantita
label.means: DOCG: Italy's guaranteed appellation, its rules set by decree.
The house founded by two brothers in the Valpantena in 1857.

records.table: Bertani's Amarone della Valpolicella Classico is the old school dry Amarone: Corvina and Rondinella from Tenuta Novare in Negrar, dried, fermented in concrete and aged at least seven years in large Slavonian oak. It tastes of morello, tea and liquorice; pour it with braised meat or hard cheese.
records.story: Two brothers of the Bertani family founded the house in 1857 in the Valpantena, the valley that runs north from Verona east of the Classico zone. As the house tells it, one of them travelled to Burgundy and learned the new ways of the vineyard and the cellar from his friend Jules Guyot (1807 to 1872), the agronomist whose name the Guyot training system carries. By its own account its Secco Bertani created a style of dry Veronese red, the house received a royal warrant from the Kingdom of Italy in 1923, and its Soave was served in London at the coronation lunch of 1937. In 1958 the Corvina vineyards of Tenuta Novare, at Arbizzano di Negrar in the Classico zone, gave the first official vintage of Bertani's Amarone. Its making is long and slow: grapes dried in lofts, fermentation in concrete and at least seven years in large Slavonian oak at the Grezzana cellar, so that the house's library of the wine runs from 1958 onwards. At the end of 2011 the brand, the Grezzana cellars and Tenuta Novare passed to the wine company of the Angelini group, while the family kept part of its land for a new estate. For a sommelier it shows the classic dry Amarone of long cask ageing, with half a century of vintages to prove how it keeps.

others.name: Secco Bertani
others.note: The house's historic dry Veronese red, a style the house says it created.

others.name: Amarone della Valpolicella Valpantena
others.note: The house's Amarone of its home valley, a named subzone of Valpolicella.

others.name: Recioto della Valpolicella Valpantena
others.note: The sweet wine of dried grapes from the same valley.

traps: Amarone is dry despite its dried grapes; Recioto della Valpolicella is the sweet one.
Valpantena is a named subzone of Valpolicella, not a separate appellation; the Classico Amarone comes from Negrar, not from the Valpantena.
The Bertani house and the Bertani family's later estate have been separate businesses since the sale of 2011.

cards.front: Bertani: which vineyards gave the first official vintage of its Amarone, and in which year?
cards.back: The Corvina vineyards of Tenuta Novare at Arbizzano di Negrar, in 1958.

cards.front: How long does Bertani's Amarone Classico age in large Slavonian oak before release?
cards.back: At least seven years, in casks of fifty to one hundred hectolitres at the Grezzana cellar.

questions.q: A guest asks how Bertani's Amarone della Valpolicella Classico is raised before release. Which answer is right?
opts: Seven years or more in large Slavonian oak
Eighteen months in new French barriques
A year in stainless steel, then bottle
Five years in clay amphorae underground
questions.exp: Bertani ferments in concrete and ages the wine at least seven years in Slavonian oak casks of fifty to one hundred hectolitres; new barriques belong to a modern style, not this one.

questions.q: Bertani was founded by two brothers in 1857. Where, by the house's account, did one of them learn the new viticulture of his day?
opts: In Bordeaux, from the Médoc brokers
In Champagne, at a house in Reims
In Piedmont, at the school of Alba
questions.exp: The house tells that the brother travelled to Burgundy and learned from his friend Jules Guyot, the agronomist of the Guyot training system; the Médoc brokers belong to Bordeaux's history, not Bertani's.

sources.title: Bertani: The Library, the vertical of Amarone della Valpolicella Classico
WineNews: the Angelini group and Bertani

report: Six searches, four of them on the house's own domains (bertani.net and library.bertani.net), which give the founding, the Guyot story, the warrant of 1923, the coronation of 1937, the first official vintage of 1958 at Tenuta Novare, the blend, the concrete vats, the cask sizes and the tasting notes.

The house's pages give the cask time as at least seven years, seven years and eight years, so the record says at least seven; the 2015 vintage dried 78 days, one year's figure, so the making says through the autumn.

The sale of 1 December 2011 to the Angelini group's wine company rests on WineNews and Blitz Quotidiano, with the family's Tenuta Santa Maria page for the land it kept; Guyot's dates on Wikipedia and the Wein.plus glossary; the DOCG of 2010 on the Valpolicella consorzio.

The founding brothers, Giovan Battista and Gaetano, are described rather than named, their dates not found; the region record's claim that Bertani was among the first to sell Amarone from the late 1950s found no independent source and is not repeated.

wine.name: Campofiorin
wine.classification: Indicazione Geografica Tipica, outside the Valpolicella DOC rules
wine.grapes: Corvina for the larger part, with Rondinella and a little Molinara.
wine.sites: Corvina, Rondinella and Molinara of the Verona hills, the country around the house's cellars in Valpolicella; as a Verona IGT the wine is not bound to one appellation's vineyards.
wine.making: The three grapes are first made into a fresh red. That wine is then refermented with whole, semi dried grapes of the same varieties, some 30 per cent by the house's figure, kept apart from the grapes for Amarone. It ages at least eighteen months in wood, mostly large casks of Slavonian oak with the rest in barrels of 600 litres, then rests some months in bottle.
wine.glass: Ripe and dried cherry with berry fruit, cinnamon and a hint of raisin from the dried grapes; round and fairly full, with soft tannin and good length.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink on release; by the house's own reckoning it keeps for fifteen to twenty years in a good cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, the house suggesting 18; open it a little ahead or decant it briefly; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The wine's own name, first made with the 1964 vintage.
A red of the Verona IGT, which the house also writes Rosso Verona; not a Valpolicella DOC.
The house, named for the Vaio dei Masi, the small valley where the family's vineyards began.

records.table: Masi's Campofiorin, first made in 1964 by refermenting a young red on the semi dried skins left from Amarone, gave the Ripasso method its name. Made since the 1980s with whole semi dried grapes, it is a Verona IGT of ripe cherry and cinnamon with soft tannin.
records.story: As the family tells it, the Boscaini family's history in wine begins in 1772 with vineyards in the Vaio dei Masi, a small valley of Valpolicella that gave the house its name, and the house has passed through seven generations of the family. In 1964 the house refermented a freshly made red of Corvina, Rondinella and Molinara on the semi dried skins left from making Amarone, and called the method Ripasso, a word it found in the old cellar talk of Valpolicella. The wine was Campofiorin, first sold in 1967 and labelled Ripasso. In 1973 Masi began to work with the Serego Alighieri counts on their wines, whose line runs back to the poet of the Divine Comedy and who have lived in Valpolicella since 1353. In the 1980s the house's technical group refined the method into a double fermentation with whole semi dried grapes in place of Amarone skins. Valpolicella Ripasso, made on the skins of Amarone or Recioto, became a DOC of its own in 2010, while Campofiorin stayed a Verona IGT, which the house calls a Supervenetian. With the 2020 vintage Masi restyled the label in a shape that recalls the 1964 one. For a sommelier it is the wine to name when a guest asks where Ripasso came from.

others.name: Costasera Amarone della Valpolicella Classico
others.note: The house's widely seen Amarone, from the Classico zone.

others.name: Mazzano Amarone della Valpolicella Classico
others.note: The single vineyard Amarone from a high, cool site.

others.name: Brolo Campofiorin Oro
others.note: A Campofiorin from a brolo, a walled vineyard, aged in smaller oak casks.

traps: Campofiorin is a Verona IGT, not a Valpolicella Ripasso DOC, though Masi gave the Ripasso method its name.
Campofiorin is refermented with whole semi dried grapes, not on Amarone skins as in the 1964 original and in Ripasso DOC.
Serego Alighieri is an estate name, not an appellation.

cards.front: Masi Campofiorin: what is the young wine refermented with?
cards.back: Whole, semi dried grapes of Corvina, Rondinella and Molinara, some 30 per cent by the house's figure, kept apart from the Amarone grapes.

cards.front: In which vintage was Masi's Campofiorin first made, the wine that gave Ripasso its name?

questions.q: A guest orders Masi's Campofiorin expecting a Valpolicella Ripasso DOC. What does its label say?
questions.exp: Campofiorin is labelled a Verona IGT; although Masi named the Ripasso method, its double fermentation with whole semi dried grapes is not the Ripasso DOC's refermentation on Amarone or Recioto skins.

questions.q: In the 1980s Masi changed how Campofiorin is made. What did the change bring in?
opts: Refermentation with whole semi dried grapes
questions.exp: Masi's technical group refined the 1964 method, which used the skins left from Amarone, into a double fermentation with whole semi dried grapes; barriques, spirit and carbonic maceration play no part.

sources.title: Masi: The history of the Boscaini family
Wine Business International: Pressure on Ripasso

report: Eight searches and one WebFetch of the house's technical sheet on media.masi.it, refused by the network and not retried; the house's own pages give 1772, the 1964 vintage, the name Ripasso, the 1980s double fermentation, the 30 per cent, the grapes, 18 degrees and fifteen to twenty years, and the 2020 restyle with The Drinks Business.
Founded is the house's own 1772, hedged in the story; the library gives no year. The man the house credits with Campofiorin, and its winemaker of 1964, are not named: their dates were not found.

The eighteen months in wood rests on Charton Hobbs and two merchants, the house's sheet being unreachable; the release of 1967 labelled Ripasso on Wine Business International and Veronissima; the Ripasso DOC of 2010 on Decanter and Italian Wine Central.
The Serego Alighieri partnership of 1973 and the family in Valpolicella since 1353 rest on Decanter China's Masi feature and Bindella; Dante is described rather than named, his dates not searched.
The house prints both Rosso del Veronese IGT and Rosso Verona IGT across its pages, so the record names the one on its product page and the label note gives the other.

The library's note on Campofiorin, the model for the modern double fermentation style, runs two things together: the 1964 wine was refermented on Amarone skins, the model for Ripasso, and the double fermentation with whole semi dried grapes is the house's refinement of the 1980s, as its own pages tell it. The sites are kept general: no source read named Campofiorin's vineyards. The library's Mazzano and Costasera notes are kept as the library gives them, and the house's 2016 report and food brochure disagree on whether 2012 or 2014 marked fifty years, so neither is used.

wine.name: Soave Classico Calvarino
wine.classification: DOC, from the historic hill zone of Soave
wine.grapes: Garganega, about seven tenths, with Trebbiano di Soave for the rest.
wine.sites: The Calvarino vineyard in the Soave Classico hills, bought by the founder in 1901: volcanic soil rich in Eocene basalt, facing north west, trained on the pergola veronese.
wine.making: Trebbiano di Soave is picked from mid September and Garganega in October, and the free run juice is fermented at cool, controlled temperatures in glass lined concrete tanks. The wine then rests on its fine lees in those tanks for about a year, stirred by hand from time to time, and a few months in bottle before release. No oak is used.
wine.glass: Wet stone and a saline, iodine note over elderflower, acacia and jasmine, with lemon and fresh almond on the finish; dry, direct and fresh, light in body but long.
wine.ageing: Taut when young, it opens over a few years and keeps for ten years and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The historic hill zone of the Soave appellation, around the town of Soave.
The vineyard's name, little Calvary, for a slope steep and hard to work.
The family house of Soave, founded in 1880.

records.table: Pieropan's Calvarino is a Soave Classico from one volcanic vineyard, bottled on its own since 1971: Garganega with Trebbiano di Soave, raised in concrete on its lees, never in oak. It tastes of wet stone, elderflower and almond; pour it cool with lake fish or risotto.
records.story: The house was founded in 1880 by the town doctor of Soave. In 1901 he bought the family's first vineyard, Calvarino, on volcanic hillside in the Classico zone; its name, little Calvary, is said to come from how steep and hard the slope was to work. By the family's account the house was among the first to print the name Soave on its labels, in the 1930s. The founder's grandson and namesake took charge in the late 1960s, after studying oenology and viticulture at Conegliano. In 1971 he bottled Calvarino on its own, by the family's account the first Italian white named for a single vineyard, and in 1978 he added La Rocca, from the hill behind Soave castle and raised in wood. Calvarino is raised instead in glass lined concrete, resting on its lees for about a year. The grandson died in April 2018 at seventy one, and his two sons carried the house on. For a sommelier the pair is a lesson in Soave: Calvarino on basalt, taut and saline, and La Rocca on limestone, the richer of the two and raised in wood, both from Garganega in the Classico hills.

others.name: Soave Classico La Rocca
others.note: Garganega from the hill behind Soave castle, raised in wood, first made under the name in 1978.

others.name: Recioto di Soave Classico Le Colombare
others.note: The sweet wine of dried Garganega, a DOCG.

others.name: Calvarino 5
others.note: Calvarino of several vintages kept for years on its fine lees before a late release.

traps: Soave is the place and Garganega the grape; Trebbiano di Soave is a different variety from Trebbiano Toscano.
Calvarino is raised in concrete without oak; it is La Rocca that is raised in wood.
Calvarino is a Soave Classico DOC; Recioto di Soave is the sweet DOCG of dried grapes.

cards.front: Pieropan Calvarino: on what soil does the vineyard lie, and how is the wine raised?
cards.back: Volcanic soil rich in basalt; it rests about a year on its lees in glass lined concrete, with no oak.

cards.front: Which Pieropan Soave comes from the hill behind Soave castle and is raised in wood?
cards.back: La Rocca, first made under that name in 1978.

questions.q: A guest compares Pieropan's two single vineyard Soaves. Which describes Calvarino?
opts: Volcanic basalt, raised in glass lined concrete
questions.exp: Calvarino grows on Eocene basalt and rests on its lees in glass lined concrete, never oak; limestone and wood belong to the house's La Rocca.

questions.q: In 1971 Pieropan bottled Calvarino on its own. What did that make it, by the family's account?
opts: The first Italian white named for one vineyard
The first Soave raised in oak
The first sparkling wine of Soave
The first Soave sold as a DOCG
questions.exp: By the family's account Calvarino was the first Italian white named for a single vineyard; the house's first Soave raised in wood was La Rocca, from 1978.

sources.title: Decanter: Soave wine pioneer Leonildo Nino Pieropan dies
Liberty Wines: Pieropan Calvarino Soave Classico

report: Four searches, three on the house's own domain, which gives 1880, the purchase of Calvarino in 1901, the 1930s labels, the grandson at Conegliano, 1971, 1978, the blend, the basalt, the aspect, the pergola, the concrete, the lees, 10 to 12 degrees and the tasting notes; the house's 1966 and late 1960s disagree, so the story says the late 1960s.

The founder and his grandson, both Leonildo Pieropan, are described rather than named: the founder's dates were not found, and the grandson's birth year is 1946 or 1947 by Decanter's age of seventy one at his death on 13 April 2018.

Little Calvary rests on Liberty Wines and a second merchant; the ten years and more on a critic's window of ten to twelve years and the house's own Calvarino 5; the first single vineyard white and the early Soave labels are the house's claims and are hedged as such.

The house's own pages give the vineyard at 95 to 145 metres and at 200 to 300 metres, so no height is given; the house also calls La Rocca the first Soave aged in wood, which the record does not repeat as a fact.
The library's Calvarino note, the first single vineyard Soave, agrees with the house's broader claim of the first Italian single vineyard white.

records.place: Santo Stefano, Valdobbiadene, Conegliano Valdobbiadene, Veneto

wine.name: Valdobbiadene Superiore di Cartizze Dry
wine.classification: DOCG since 2009; a subzone with its own rules since 1969
wine.grapes: Glera, the Prosecco grape: alone, by the house's sheets, where the appellation asks for at least 85 per cent.
wine.sites: The family's parcels on the Cartizze hill at Santo Stefano di Valdobbiadene: a steep crest near 300 metres, sunny and sheltered from cold winds, on crumbly soil over rock.
wine.making: The grapes are pressed gently and cold, and the must settles cold for about a week before fermenting in stainless steel. The base wine rests on its lees, then makes its second fermentation in sealed pressure tanks, the Martinotti method, for at least thirty days, with no malolactic conversion, and is finished Dry.
wine.glass: Apricot, white peach and green apple with acacia blossom and pear; a soft mousse and a gentle sweetness held in balance by fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, while its fruit and blossom are fresh; it is not a wine to lay down.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip shaped white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: From the one hill of Cartizze above Valdobbiadene, the subzone at the head of the appellation.
Despite the word, softly sweet: sweeter than Brut and Extra Dry.
The guaranteed appellation of the Conegliano Valdobbiadene hills, since 2009.

records.table: Bisol's Cartizze is Prosecco Superiore from the one hill of Cartizze above Valdobbiadene, where the family's records go back to 1542. It is Glera made in pressure tanks and finished Dry, so softly sweet with apricot, white peach and acacia: pour it cold as an aperitif or with fruit tarts.
records.story: By the family's account its records in Santo Stefano di Valdobbiadene go back to 1542, and it has owned land on the Cartizze hill since then. At the start of the twentieth century a forebear built a thriving wine trade, broken off by the First World War; his son revived it in the mid 1920s and, after the Second World War, travelled the hills of Valdobbiadene and Conegliano to buy plots. The land gained its law on 2 April 1969, when the Ministry of Agriculture recognised Conegliano Valdobbiadene as a DOC, with Superiore di Cartizze as a subzone of its own. In 2009 the hills were raised to DOCG, and the grape was renamed Glera so that Prosecco could be protected as the name of a place. Cartizze is one sheltered crest between the hamlets of San Pietro di Barbozza, Santo Stefano and Saccol, divided among many owners, and its wine is usually finished Dry, softer and sweeter than the Brut of the wider hills. In 2014 Bisol became part of the Lunelli group. For a sommelier the wine teaches two things a guest gets wrong: that a Prosecco can name a single hill, and that Dry on its label means softly sweet.

others.name: Relio Rive di Guia
others.note: A Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore from the Rive of Guia, one of the appellation's named hillsides.

others.name: Crede
others.note: A Valdobbiadene Prosecco Superiore DOCG of the house's hill vineyards.

traps: Cartizze labelled Dry is sweeter than Brut and Extra Dry, not drier.
Cartizze is a hill shared by many owners, not one producer's vineyard.
Prosecco Superiore is made sparkling in pressure tanks, not by the traditional method of Champagne.

cards.front: Bisol's Cartizze is labelled Dry. How sweet is it?
cards.back: Softly sweet, sweeter than Brut and Extra Dry: Dry is one of the sweeter styles of Prosecco.

cards.front: When did the Cartizze subzone of Bisol's flagship first gain legal recognition?
cards.back: On 2 April 1969, within the Conegliano Valdobbiadene DOC; the hills became DOCG in 2009.

questions.q: A guest asks for a bone dry Prosecco and points to Bisol's Cartizze Dry. What do you tell them?
opts: It is softly sweet, sweeter than Brut
It is the driest style, below Brut Nature
It is a still wine, not sparkling
It is made by the traditional method
questions.exp: Dry is a sweeter style than Extra Dry and Brut, and Cartizze is usually finished Dry; for a bone dry wine offer a Brut instead.

questions.q: Conegliano Valdobbiadene, with Superiore di Cartizze as its subzone, was first recognised as a DOC in which year?
questions.exp: The Ministry of Agriculture recognised the DOC on 2 April 1969; 2009 is the year the hills became DOCG and the grape took the name Glera.

sources.title: Consorzio Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco: the Consortium
Italian Wine Central: Conegliano Valdobbiadene Prosecco DOCG

report: Five searches: the house's own domain gives 1542, the forebear's trade and the First World War, the son's revival in the mid 1920s, the land on Cartizze since 1542, the Lunelli group in 2014, the site, the soil and the tasting notes; the fact sheets on a distributor's host give the pressing, the steel, the thirty days in pressure tanks, no malolactic and Glera alone.

Founded is left empty, as in the library: 1542 is the family's oldest record, not a founding, and no source read gave a year for the business; the forebear and his son, Eliseo and Desiderio Bisol, are described rather than named, their dates not found.
The DOC of 2 April 1969 rests on the consorzio; the DOCG of 2009 on Italian Wine Central and Drinks International; the renaming to Glera on Wikipedia and the Wine Scholar Guild.

The house's own spec sheet gives Glera at 85 per cent at the least and its fact sheets give Glera alone, so the record says both; the house's holding on Cartizze is given by two of its own pages in different figures, so none is given.
The ageing line, to drink young, rests on the tank method and the house's sheets giving no ageing; no source read gave a drinking window, so a checker may wish to confirm it.
